summary: Presents the Softwire Mesh framework for carrying IPv4 and IPv6 across single-protocol networks, such as ones that handle only IPv4 or only IPv6. The goal is for both to work on the Internet as the transition takes place.

eli5.summary: Some networks speak only the old addresses and some only the new. This framework uses tunnels so both kinds of traffic can cross the other's territory.

questions: how to carry ipv6 over an ipv4 only core
how to carry ipv4 over an ipv6 only core
subtitle: A framework for carrying IPv4 across IPv6-only cores, and IPv6 across IPv4-only cores, using BGP routes and tunnels called softwires.

tldr.problem: Some backbone networks will understand only IPv4 or only IPv6, yet they must still carry transit traffic for the other protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Edge routers that speak both protocols (AFBRs) exchange the other protocol's routes over IBGP running on the core's native protocol, and tunnel the other protocol's packets across the core in softwires.
tldr.outcome: The framework does not mandate one tunneling technology, and it says where existing technology is enough and where new signaling or multicast work is needed.

facts.label: Tunnel mesh size
facts.value: N^2 point-to-point tunnels for N AFBRs

facts.label: IPsec on softwires
facts.value: ESP with null encryption or AH

today: RFC 5565 is a Proposed Standard from June 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Tunnel Across a Single-Protocol Core
sections.content:
A backbone normally distributes internal routes with an IGP such as OSPF or IS-IS and external routes with BGP. With native forwarding every interior router needs the external routes. With tunneled forwarding the ingress router wraps the packet in an encapsulation header addressed to the egress router, so interior (P) routers only need internal routes. This is sometimes called a BGP-free core.

This framework applies the idea to two cases: an IPv6-only core carrying IPv4, and an IPv4-only core carrying IPv6. The edge routers must handle both families and are called Address Family Border Routers (AFBRs). The tunnels are softwires. The RFC is explicit about which pieces can use existing technology and which need new or modified technology.
sections.eli5: Inner roads only know one kind of address. So the border stations wrap each foreign parcel in a box with an address the inner roads understand.

sections.title: Scenarios and Terms: E-IP and I-IP
sections.content:
In the IPv6-over-IPv4 scenario the client networks run IPv6 and the backbone runs IPv4. In the IPv4-over-IPv6 scenario it is reversed. The RFC assumes there may be 'backdoor' connections between client networks, so the routing solution must work in any topology. It notes that IPv4-over-IPv6 is a significant emerging need because some providers are building IPv6 backbones without native IPv4 in their core routers.

To talk about both at once, the RFC uses I-IP (Internal IP) for the family the transit core supports and E-IP (External IP) for the family the clients use. E-IP is IPv4 exactly when I-IP is IPv6. P routers support only I-IP, CE routers only E-IP, and AFBRs both, with I-IP on core-facing interfaces and E-IP on client-facing ones.
sections.eli5: Inside the island they speak one language (I-IP), outside another (E-IP). Border stations speak both.

sections.title: Distributing E-IP Routes Between AFBRs
sections.content:
P routers and AFBRs run an IGP for I-IP routes. AFBRs use IBGP to exchange E-IP routes, either in a full mesh or through a BGP Route Reflector. The IBGP sessions run over I-IP and are not tunneled; the BGP next hop for each E-IP route is an I-IP address.

Encoding a next hop from a different family than the NLRI is not obvious. RFC 4798 explains it for IPv6 routes with an IPv4 next hop, and RFC 5549 for IPv4 routes with an IPv6 next hop. A speaker advertising itself as next hop MUST, unless policy overrides, use the I-IP family, and a Route Reflector MUST NOT change the next hop's family. If a BGP capability is defined for this case, all AFBRs in a transit core MUST advertise it.

The address an AFBR uses as BGP next hop must match the address it is known by to its tunneling technology. Using labeled IPv4 or IPv6 address families so packets carry an MPLS label is OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: The border stations tell each other where parcels should go using the inner island's own language, never inside boxes.

sections.title: Forwarding Through a Softwire
sections.content:
An ingress AFBR looks up an E-IP packet's destination. The best match will be a BGP route whose next hop is the I-IP address of the egress AFBR. The ingress encapsulates the packet with a header the P routers can process, and the egress removes it and forwards by the payload's destination. The decision to use a softwire is policy at the ingress, for example when the BGP next hop is an I-IP address. The packet MUST be sent through a softwire whose remote endpoint address equals the BGP next hop address.

Encapsulation always makes the packet longer. The MTU of the softwire path SHOULD be large enough that no packet is fragmented before or during encapsulation.

Choice of tunneling technology is also policy. The framework accommodates MPLS (LDP or RSVP-TE), L2TPv3, GRE, IP-in-IP and IPsec. Routers can advertise class memberships so policy can say 'use L2TPv3 to routers in class X', using RFC 5512.
sections.eli5: The first border station looks up the exit station, seals the parcel in a box addressed to it, and the exit station opens the box and delivers the parcel.

sections.title: Softwire Signaling
sections.content:
A full mesh of softwires between N AFBRs would need N^2 point-to-point tunnels. Manual configuration of such tunnels is not part of the framework. Because the core provides layer 3 transit, multipoint-to-point tunnels are enough, matching native IP where the egress cannot tell which router sent a packet. Softwires are meant to be always on.

Where a technology has native signaling, it is used: LDP or RSVP-TE for MPLS, and IKEv2 with IPsec for IPsec softwires. For GRE and L2TPv3 the signaling is BGP-based and described in RFC 5512. IP-in-IP and GRE without options need no signaling, since the egress address is already distributed by BGP. Fields such as TTL and DSCP in the outer header are set by policy at the ingress.
sections.eli5: Some box types come with their own rules for setting up a route, and some need a new set of rules. The simplest types only need the exit station's address.

sections.title: Multicast, OAM and Multiple ASes
sections.content:
For multicast, the RFC supports PIM-SM and PIM-SSM across the core, not BIDIR-PIM, BSR or AutoRP. In the one-to-one scheme each client tree maps to one core tree. With PIM in the core, the AFBR translates the PIM message and adds an RPF Vector (RFC 5496) because core routers lack routes to the source. With mLDP, client SSM trees map onto P2MP LSPs, but this cannot be used for sparse mode groups. MVPN-like schemes from L3VPN multicast treat the AFBRs as PE routers of one VPN, and can support SM, SSM and Bidir groups.

For OAM, softwire endpoints can be monitored with BGP/TCP timeouts, ICMP or LSP echo, or BFD. A softwire echo mechanism is also suggested. The RFC says new or extended MIBs will be needed.

If a transit core spans several ASes, the remote softwire endpoint is not the BGP next hop, so the procedures do not work as written. Options include requiring AFBRs at each AS edge, using multi-hop EBGP, or having non-AFBR ASBRs leave the next hop unchanged. The latter two need recursive next hop resolution and possibly stacked encapsulations.
sections.eli5: Group broadcasts, health checks and crossing several countries each need extra rules, and the document sketches the options rather than fixing one.

sections.title: Security of the Encapsulation
sections.content:
The payload packets have the same security needs whether or not they travel through a softwire, so the concern is the encapsulation header, which must be in the clear. Without authentication, attackers can spoof or replay encapsulated packets. They cannot redirect the payload to another address, but they can side-step policy about what enters a softwire. Cryptography cannot fully stop denial-of-service floods, since checking spoofed packets costs more.

Within one administrative domain, border filtering of tunnel addresses or MPLS packets can help, as can a cleartext password such as the 64-bit cookie of L2TPv3. For wider use, a control protocol MUST have authentication, and BGP's MD5 mechanism is satisfactory when BGP sets up the tunnel. Data SHOULD be secured with IPsec; it MUST provide authentication and integrity, using ESP with null encryption or AH. Keys MUST be distributed automatically with IKEv2.
sections.eli5: The outside of each box can be read by anyone, so a stranger could fake a box. Inside one trusted area you can guard the doors; between areas you need a proper lock and key.
